newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Manuel cautious on S.African privatisation cash.
newsitem.headline: Manuel cautious on S.African privatisation cash.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Thursday his budget had been conservative on proceeds from the sale of state assets in 1997/98 but some would be used to retire state debt.

"On the utilisaition of proceeds...there is a choice between debt retirement and infrastructure rollouts, and it is going to be hard to develop a single set of rules across the board," he told parliament's finance committee.

Referring to the imminent sale of a 30 percent stake of telecoms group Telkom to SBC Communications and Telekom Malaysia, Manuel said there were too many variables to say how much would go to central government.
"Telkom is negotiating with a consortium. Out of those negotiations will come a price. Far be it from us to determine what that price will be," he said.

Analysts estimate the sale, due to be concluded next month, could net the government some six billion rand. But even after a price was agreed, it remained to be seen how much of the money would be ploughed into improving Telkom's infrastructure, particularly in deprived areas, Manuel said.
The balance between building infrastructure and cutting debt would vary from privatisation to privatisation, he added.
In Telkom's case the need to extend telephone lines to deprived areas might result in a higher retention of receipts for spending in the industry.
"We want that infrastructure rollout so what may happen there is the retention of a lot more than in the case of another kind of entity."

Manuel's budget, unveiled on Wednesday, made no provisions for privatisation receipts in cutting the 1997/98 borrowing requirement, apart from 516 million rand earned from the sale of six SABC radio stations last year.

That disappointed some analysts who had argued the government could use up to five billion rand from the sale of stakes in Telkom and other state assets -- such as Sun Air, the Airports Company and leisure group Aventura -- to reduce its expected gros borrowing requirement of 36.8 billion rand.
